brief.text: The state is not a set of institutions, Ajay Shah said, citing Max Weber, but a community of people holding a monopoly of physical violence over a territory. {033-C02}

brief.head: If Nehru were alive
brief.text: Freedom fighters chased principle because power was not on offer, Amit Varma said. “If Nehru was alive today, I posit that he would be Pratap Bhanu Mehta.” {033-C04}

brief.head: Less money, more good
brief.text: Indian economists generally favour bigger government, Ajay Shah said. Yet sceptics of state spending might conclude that “the Indian state would do more good if it had less money”. {033-C06}

brief.head: When in doubt, ban it
brief.text: Indian officials ban what is hard to understand or risky, Ajay Shah said: doing good goes unrewarded, while getting into trouble “will destroy your career”. {033-C15}

brief.head: The booth knows
brief.text: Results are visible booth by booth, about 2,000 people each, Ajay Shah said, so a winning party can reward or punish a whole basti. {033-C21}

thought.text: Governments consist of people, right? And people respond to incentives.
thought.who: Amit Varma, stating the core truth of public choice theory, which he felt should not need saying

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah apply economics to the state
lead.head: The state, minus the halo
body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah opened the episode bench pressing. “Put effort. Put effort,” Varma urged. The heavier lifting was intellectual: why the state so often fails the people it is meant to serve.
Their tool was public choice theory, which Varma called his favourite branch of economics. It applies the study of how people respond to incentives to politicians, bureaucrats, voters and the state.
Its core truth, he said, should not need saying: government is “not some mythical benevolent beast sitting up there”. Governments consist of people, and people respond to incentives. {033-C01}
There is no single public interest, Varma argued, only different people wanting different things. That matters in a country whose biggest religion, he said, is the religion of government.
Shah framed the episode as the third pillar of a series on the state, after episodes on what a state is and what it should do.
## Follow the incentives
Politicians want, above all, to get elected, Varma said. “This automatically means that a politician’s time horizon is always a short term. It is the next election.” {033-C03}
So they cater to popular sentiment, and neglect policies whose payoff is long-term or rests on counterintuitive truths, such as the idea that life is positive-sum.

Special interests supply the money politicians need, and expect a return. The public seldom notices, because each person loses a rupee while a few gain enormously: concentrated benefits, diffuse costs.
Shah added a twist. “The one thing worse than a world where private firms can lobby with the government and influence policy is one in which they cannot,” he said.

Bureaucrats, Varma said, are mostly good people, his own father among them. But they protect and expand their turf. “You are on a gravy train, you want that gravy train to continue as long as possible.” {033-C12}
Shah warned that India is becoming an administrative state, where officials rule and citizens are subjects.
## Ballots and blind spots
Voters fare no better. One vote almost never decides an election, so it is rational not to study manifestos, Varma said, citing Anthony Downs’s idea of rational ignorance. {033-C16}
“Voting doesn’t affect me in the everyday,” he said. Shah went further: he has never voted, because the cost-benefit analysis never made sense to him.
Varma also weighed first-past-the-post, under which, he said, a party with 35 per cent of the votes can win 80 per cent of the seats, against proportional representation, without picking a side.
## The rulebook
The incentives, Varma said, come from how the state is designed, and the constitution writes the rules of the game.
His test of a good system is whether the worst person in the world could come to power and still do little damage, because the state simply lacks the power. {033-C22}
India’s Constitution, he argued, protects the state more than the citizen. Shah said he was not that unhappy with the state of affairs, placing his hopes in the basic structure doctrine.
Shah signed off calling public choice disconcerting, but “the cold reality of the world that we should think of the state as an optimizing bunch of people”.

second.label: The public purse
second.head: Other people’s money
second.deck: Amit Varma borrows Milton Friedman’s matrix to show how governments spend
body: Amit Varma reached for a matrix drawn up by the economist Milton Friedman. Spend your own money on yourself, and you economise and seek value. Spend it on a stranger, and you economise but hardly care about value.

Spend someone else’s money on yourself, and you seek value but do not economise. Spend somebody else’s money on somebody else, and you do neither. “This is the whole business of government,” Varma said. {033-C05}

Ajay Shah added PJ O’Rourke’s line that giving money and power to politicians is like giving whiskey and car keys to teenagers. {033-J05} Varma raised him HL Mencken: every election is “a sort of an advanced auction sale of stolen goods”.

quote.text: And if I spend somebody else’s money on somebody else, I will neither economize nor seek value.

second.caption: the four ways to spend money

third.head: A bad bet on online poker
body: Sheldon Adelson owned physical casinos, among them the Sands and the Venetian. For many years, Amit Varma said, he lobbied to keep online poker banned, and he was one of the big funders of the Republican Party.
Varma, who has been a professional poker player, watched from the inside. Adelson, he said, was much hated among poker professionals. He believed online poker threatened his casinos.
“Actually, it is kinda ironic that it really wasn’t,” Varma said. “It’s just that the ecosystem of gambling expanded when online poker came in. It didn’t hurt the live casinos.” {033-S02}

Such capture by special interests is far worse in the US than in India, Varma said, recommending Jonathan Rauch’s *Government’s End* as “a scary read”. India is not there yet, he said, but could easily get there. {033-R06}

sections.label: The premise
sections.head: No benevolent beast
sections.caption: governments as people
body: Public choice theory, Amit Varma said, is his favourite branch of economics. It takes the study of how people respond to incentives under scarcity and applies it to politics: politicians, bureaucracy, elections, voting and the state.
Its core truth seems obvious, he said, but needs saying anyway. Government is not a benevolent being; governments consist of people, who are “frail”, “flawed” and “often rational”. {033-C01}
Nor is there a public interest for them to serve, he said: different people want different things. “There is no aggregated thing.”
## A community with guns

Ajay Shah brought in Max Weber. The state, in Weber’s definition, is not a collection of institutions but “a community of people that achieve and maintain the monopoly of physical violence on a territory”. {033-C02}

Rule-bound, predictable institutions are an aspiration, Shah said, and every government achieves them to a different degree. So the economist should ask what the people inside the state are maximising, and predict how they will wield its coercive power.
Varma added a caution. Even “community” is too collective: a community does not have values, only the people within it do.
~ This matters most in India, he argued, where the biggest religion is the religion of government, and *Mai Baap Sarkar* is expected to solve every problem. {033-J15}

quote.text: There is no such thing as a public interest.

sections.label: Politicians
sections.head: Thinking only till polling day
sections.caption: the politician’s short horizon
body: The number one incentive of a politician, Amit Varma said, is to get elected. So the time horizon is always the next election, and a party leader always faces a local election somewhere. {033-C03}

Good policies often rest on counterintuitive insights: that life is positive-sum, not zero-sum, and that markets, languages and natural selection work by bottom-up evolution. People are conditioned instead to want a strong leader who, if prices are too high, says: “I will fix the price.”
He also recalled a famous cartoon: two wolves and a sheep, voting on what to have for dinner.
## Spending without care
Politicians control enormous sums, and by Milton Friedman’s matrix, Varma said, those who spend somebody else’s money on somebody else neither economise nor seek value. {033-C05}

Varma claims to have written the first public choice limerick, for his weekly slot in the *Times of India*: “A neta who loves currency notes / told me what his line of work denotes. / It is kind of funny, / we steal people’s money / and use some of it to buy their votes.” {033-J01}
~ Asked by Ajay Shah whether this was before ChatGPT, Varma said ChatGPT cannot write limericks “because it can’t count”: a good limerick needs nine, nine, six, six and nine syllables. {033-J02}

quote.text: We steal people’s money and use some of it to buy their votes.

sections.label: Special interests
sections.head: Your rupee, their windfall
sections.caption: concentrated benefits and diffuse costs
body: Politicians need tons of money, Amit Varma said, and special interests supply it as an investment that will need a return, usually through policies that shield them from competition or redistribute wealth to them.

The public does not notice because of a phenomenon Varma credited to Mancur Olson: concentrated benefits and diffuse costs. If the government took one rupee from everyone and gave it to Ajay Shah, “everybody who’s losing one rupee, they don’t even know they’re losing one rupee”. {033-C08}
Shah, meanwhile, would be getting “one point seven billion rupees or whatever it is”, and would gladly give his local politician ten per cent. {#billion}
Small traders, voters and funders for some parties, can keep FDI out of retail, and consumers pay more for less without noticing.
## Worse than lobbying

Shah complicated the picture. In London, New York or Tokyo, he said, firms openly lobby and disagree with officials, which disperses power. In India, regulators hold arbitrary power and industry has been coerced into silence. “The one thing worse than a world where private firms can lobby with the government and influence policy is one in which they cannot.” {033-C11}
~ Varma agreed, but put the deeper problem elsewhere: in an ideal world, the state would not have the power to block entry into a market at all.

quote.text: Which is why I say all interventions in free markets are redistributions from the poor to the rich.

sections.label: Bureaucrats
sections.head: All aboard the gravy train
sections.caption: bureaucrats and their turf
body: Amit Varma’s father was an IAS officer, “a good man”, and “perhaps a little too honest, or completely honest”. So Varma rejects the stereotype of the corrupt babu: most bureaucrats are good people responding to incentives. {033-S07}

He found those incentives in *Parkinson’s Law*, by C Northcote Parkinson, a classic of comedy that is also a public choice book. Work expands to fill the time available; officials multiply subordinates, not rivals, and grow their budgets and turf. {033-R07}
The result is resistance to change and a status quo bias. Someone who would agree from outside that a ministry should be abolished, Varma said, will defend it once inside.
## Not just suitcases

Ajay Shah described an administrative state, in which the legislature and the judiciary stop acting as checks and officials rule over subjects. That, he said, is the problem India faces today. {033-C13}

He blamed Bollywood for reducing corruption to suitcases of cash. His own definition: doing things not aligned with the organisation’s professional objectives for personal gain. {033-C14} That covers favours to friends and family, career-boosting expediency and laziness: “You get the power of a civil servant and you do no work.”
~ His remedy is more democracy, he said: real checks and balances, and many sources of power outside government, so that officials feel the burn when things go wrong.

quote.text: The administrative state is one in which power gets concentrated into the officials.

sections.label: Voters
sections.head: The rationally ignorant voter
sections.caption: rational ignorance
body: Ajay Shah called elections “the great temple of the Amar Chitra Katha version of democracy”. Amit Varma began instead with Bollywood: the film *Newton*, in which Rajkummar Rao’s election officer finds that the people who turn up do not care who is on the ballot. {033-S04}
That, Varma said, is Anthony Downs’s rational ignorance. One vote almost never decides an election, so it is rational to spend scarce time and attention elsewhere. {033-C16}

A listener once corrected him: a local election in India had been decided by one vote, and the loser’s wife had not gone to vote. His advice: “kindly if your spouse is in an election, kindly vote.” {033-S05}
## Votes for sale
Tactical voting hides people’s true preferences, Varma said, citing Kenneth Arrow’s impossibility theorem: a political marketplace cannot satisfy them.

Shah added that Vitalik Buterin had told them it is too easy to bribe people to vote against their interest. In India, Shah said, politics goes one basti at a time, and “the highest bidder gets those votes”. {033-S09}
~ Why vote at all? Out of a norm, Varma said, like signalling a left turn on an empty road, “unless you’re in Bombay and you drive like me”. {033-J10}

quote.text: You vote for the same reason that you go to a Manchester United game.

sections.label: The constitution
sections.head: A state too weak to harm
sections.caption: the rules of the game
body: Public choice, Amit Varma said, teaches the most important thing of all: the rules of the game. Incentives come from the design of the state, and the constitution sets that design.

A good constitution protects people from the state. India’s, written when it was unclear whether the princely states would join, centralised power and copied the colonial state, he said. Free speech gets lip service, hedged by caveats such as public order and decency. {033-C23}

Every government from Nehru onwards, he said, amended the Constitution whenever it wanted to do something unconstitutional. He recalled a cartoon in which the Parliament bookshop stocks only books, “not periodicals”. {033-J12}
## The elite’s document

Ajay Shah doubted that successful constitutions reflect the consensus Buchanan and Tullock wanted. Most are elite projects, he said; the German and Japanese ones were partly imposed. Varma interjected: “Elite rather than elitist.”

India, Shah said, “lucked out and got a fairly bad document”. {033-J13} Its real constitution is the basic structure, which the judiciary has mostly defended, while the rest is amended like any other law. {033-C24}
~ That pushes India, he argued, towards something like the British unwritten tradition, where the work lies in applying the basic structure doctrine wisely.

quote.text: So you have a relatively liberal constitution imposed on an illiberal society by a bunch of unelected people.

side.boxText: Many date the field, Amit Varma said, to James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock’s *The Calculus of Consent* in 1962. His own way in, his “gateway drug”, was Eamonn Butler’s *Public Choice: A Primer*, masterful and readable in under an hour. {033-R01}

contQuote.text: The best system that I can think of is a system in which the worst person in the world, and Adolf Hitler even, can get to power and not manage to do any damage

p3.title: Tales of the state
p3.deck: Bootleggers, bribes, an unbought shirt and a reform that nearly happened

stories.start: There's another great phrase which I find really amusing, which has a Bollywood connection.
stories.end: Yatrakaro in you know, I will dance at your wedding also.
stories.caption: Shah Rukh Khan’s bootlegger
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s quiz: Shah Rukh Khan and public choice theory
stories.head: Raees picks the wrong fight
body: Amit Varma had a quiz question for Ajay Shah: what does Shah Rukh Khan’s film *Raees* have to do with public choice theory? Shah did not know, and had not seen the film. “Good,” said Varma. {033-S03}

In the film, Shah Rukh Khan plays a macho bootlegger in Gujarat, where alcohol is banned. One day a politician sets out on a *Darubandi Yatra*, a rally demanding that alcohol be banned, and the bootlegger wants to stop him.
This, Varma said, makes no rational sense, “because actually the bootlegger and the politician who wants alcohol banned, their interests are the same, they’re on the same side.”

There is a phrase for it, bootleggers and Baptists, coined by the regulatory economist Bruce Yandle. The Baptist says alcohol is evil, that it breaks families apart, and must be banned. “So the Baptist gets alcohol banned,” Varma said. “So alcohol is banned, and then the bootlegger comes in.” {033-C10}
The bootlegger supplies the banned *daru*. The two work for the same ends, Varma said, and sometimes they are literally hand in hand.
So in his version, the Shah Rukh character would back the politician instead: “*Yatra karo*, I will dance at your wedding also.” {033-J04}

~ The same logic hides behind many pious-sounding rules, Varma said. We think a ban on FDI in retail protects small traders, while “your money is being taken away and given to those guys”. The answer is to dig: “You got to ask why is this happening.”
stories.why: Moral crusaders and those who profit from a ban can look like enemies and still be quiet allies. Before trusting a regulation that sounds pious, ask who gains from it, and how.
stories.postscript: Varma once ran a column, *Housefull Economics*, explaining economics through films, and asked viewers whether they would like a regular segment on the show.

stories.start: We've spoken about this friend of mine who owned a restaurant in Bangalore
stories.end: the poor guy, you know, no matter how many doors he has
stories.caption: the restaurant’s doors
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on rent-seeking, one restaurant at a time
stories.head: Too many doors, too few doors
body: A friend of Amit Varma’s owned a restaurant in Bangalore. The fire department told him he needed multiple entrances. The excise department told him he could have only one, so that it could track alcohol going in and out. {033-S01}
“And all of them are taking bribes from the poor guy,” Varma said, “no matter how many doors he has.”

This, Varma said, is rent-seeking, a term that has nothing to do with renting out property. When the state controls something or creates an artificial scarcity, it can make a lot of money off it. {033-C07}
~ His hypothetical was closer to home: a government that decides podcasters need a licence, renewable every six months. “And of course I have to pay a bribe for it.” {033-J03}
stories.why: When the state controls permissions and its rules contradict each other, no one can comply, whatever they do. That impossibility is exactly what officials can charge for. Varma explored restaurant regulation further in an episode of *The Seen and the Unseen* with Madhu Menon.

stories.start: Now, what has been proposed in the past uh and almost got through
stories.end: tallest intellectuals in this country today, you know, having opposite views
stories.caption: proportional representation
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the electoral reform India nearly adopted
stories.head: The reform that almost got through
body: Jayaprakash Narayan, Amit Varma recalled from an old episode of *The Seen and the Unseen*, almost got India to adopt proportional representation. He had friends in high places, and when the UPA was in charge all the principal players had agreed. {033-R18}
Then Sonia Gandhi said no. Her sense, Varma said, was that Congress would be in power forever under first-past-the-post, and the change would hurt it.
“Now the irony of that,” Varma said, “is that had proportional representation got through the BJP would not be so dominant today and the Congress would have many more seats than they do.” {033-S06}
~ Varma did not take a side. Pratap Bhanu Mehta, he said, told him it would be an absolute disaster that would tear the country apart. Varma counts both men among the country’s tallest intellectuals.
stories.why: Those who block a reform because they think their power is permanent can end up harmed by that choice. And electoral design is genuinely contested, even among the wisest people. {033-C19}
stories.postscript: Ajay Shah noted that post-war Germany, designing against another Hitler, chose proportional representation after much debate. {033-S08}

stories.start: But leaving that aside, one interesting question I got hit with.
stories.end: that is an example of successful political entrepreneurship that happened then
stories.caption: the shirt nobody bought
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on not voting as a signal
stories.head: Nothing on the rack worth buying
body: Amit Varma once skipped an election. No party seemed worth voting for, and he did not want to vote tactically for the least evil. Someone told him that, not having voted, he should have no opinion on the result.
He disagreed strongly. If every shirt in a mall is bad, he said, you need not buy one. “My not buying a shirt is a signal that there is a gap in the market and maybe that can be fulfilled.” {033-S10}
The many Indians who do not vote, he argued, signal to political entrepreneurs that existing parties are not meeting demand.

~ That, he said, is exactly what the Aam Aadmi Party did. Varma does not like AAP, but calls it a remarkably successful exercise in political entrepreneurship: it offered disaffected middle-class voters someone like them, talking about corruption.
stories.why: Staying away from the polls is information too. Gaps in the political market get filled by new entrants, for better or worse: corruption, Varma noted, is the first rallying cry of populist movements.
stories.postscript: Ajay Shah has never voted: the cost-benefit analysis, he said, never made sense to him. {033-J11}

quiz.q: What does the Shah Rukh Khan film *Raees* get wrong about public choice, according to Varma?
quiz.a: Its bootlegger fights a prohibitionist who is really on his side.

quiz.q: Why did a Bangalore restaurant owner pay bribes whatever number of doors he had?
quiz.a: The fire department wanted many entrances, excise only one, and all took bribes.

quiz.q: In Milton Friedman’s matrix, what happens when you spend somebody else’s money on somebody else?
quiz.a: You neither economise nor seek value: the whole business of government, Varma said.

quiz.q: Which regulatory economist coined the phrase ‘bootleggers and Baptists’, according to Amit Varma?
quiz.a: Bruce Yandle, whose phrase pairs the moralist with the man who profits.

quiz.q: Why, by Anthony Downs’s idea of rational ignorance, do voters not study party manifestos?
quiz.a: One vote almost never decides an election, so attention is better spent elsewhere.

quiz.q: Why has Ajay Shah never voted in an election, by his own account?
quiz.a: He never felt the cost-benefit analysis made sense; why people vote mystifies him.
